title: Action Plan for Your Nonprofit: Growing Your Nonprofit
body:
✅ GRANT READINESS & STRATEGIC PLANNING

Course Checklist & Action Guide

Now that your nonprofit is legally established, use this checklist to register for funding portals, build your credibility profiles, and master the grant application cycle.

📌 Step 1: Verify Good Standing

  • Before applying for funds, ensure your state status is active and compliant.

    • 🔍 Check State Corporation Condition: → Verify your status with your Secretary of State to ensure you are in "Good Standing."

🏛 Step 2: Federal & Agency Registrations

  • You cannot receive federal funds without these specific registrations.

    • 💻 SAM.gov (System for Award Management) → Visit SAM.gov (Essential for federal grants & getting your Unique Entity ID)

    • 💻 Grants.gov → Visit Grants.gov (The primary database for federal opportunities) 💻

    • Dun & Bradstreet → Lookup or Request DUNS® Number

    • 💻 eRA Commons → Visit eRA Commons (Required specifically for Health and Human Service Grants)

🏅 Step 3: Build Credibility & Credentials

  • Funders check these databases to verify your legitimacy and transparency.

    • 📜 State Solicitation License → Check with your State Charity Official (Required in many states to legally ask for donations).

    • 🌟 GuideStar / Candid Listing → Claim your profile on GuideStar (Upload your determination letter and mission).

    • 🌟 Charity Navigator → Visit Charity Navigator (Get Your Rating, and monitor that rating and transparency score).

    • 🌟 Policy Commons → Visit Policy Commons (For research and policy-focused organizations).

🏘 Step 4: Access Local Funding

  • Local money is often easier to get than federal money.

    • 📍 Community & Economic Development / CDBG → Locate your County Portal for "Community Block Grants." → Contact your local Office of Community Development.

🕵 Step 5: Competitive Intelligence (FOIA Requests)

  • Don't guess how to win; copy what works. Use the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) or State Public Records Acts to see who won previously.

    • 📄 Submit a Request for Proposals (RFP) Inquiry Ask for the records of the most recent completed program year. What to request (based on the CPRA template):

  1. The Final List: Funded projects, award amounts, and descriptions.

  2. Board Items: Staff reports and approving votes.

  3. The Scoring Rubric: See exactly how the winners were graded.

  4. Award Letters: Official notifications sent to funded entities.

  5. The "Winner's" Application: Ask for a copy of the winning grant proposal to use as a model.

📝 Step 6: Master the Scoring Rubric

Every grant is a game for points. Structure your proposal to hit the maximum marks. Typical Point Distribution (Reference):

  • Project Description: ~30 Points (Design and Partners)

  • Results & Sustainability: ~30 Points (Outputs, Outcomes, Long-term benefits)

  • Statement of Need: ~18 Points (Community description, Workforce needs)

  • Budget & Narrative: ~12 Points (Alignment of costs with the project)

  • Capacity: ~10 Points (Financial documentation and Resumes)

🧠 Step 7: Tailor Your Narrative (Funder Psychology)

Different funders want different things. Customize your "Ask" based on who they are. 🏛 Local Governments:

  • Concern: Duplication of services.

  • Want: To save money and make a big local impact.

🏛 State Governments:

  • Concern: Tax savings, health, and justice.

  • Want: To see partnerships.

🏛 Federal Governments:

  • Concern: Documentation and systems.

  • Want: Structure, data capture, and reproducibility.

🏢 Corporations:

  • Concern: Their brand story.

  • Want: To know how the grant changes individual lives (faces and feelings).

🗓 Step 8: The Grant Calendar

Grants move in cycles. Use this schedule to prepare ahead of time.

  • ❄ Beginning of Year (Jan/Feb) → Source: Corporate Grants → Action: Contact project coordinators immediately. [Banks, Credit Unions]

  • 🌸 Springtime (and year-round) → Source: Foundations → Action: Get on their newsletter lists; introduce yourself to program officers.

  • 🌞 May - July → Source: Federal Grants → Action: Search Grants.gov keywords describing your work. Look at last year's release dates to predict this year's. {JUNE (sp.): Source: Tourism Authority, School Districts, Law Enforcement Fleet Management, Federal, State, & Local Auctions → Action: GET AHEAD OF THE AUCTION CYCLE}

  • 🍎 September → Source: Closing and Opening Federal Grants. Banks Second Round of Giving. → Action: Search Grants.gov keywords describing your work. Contact project coordinators immediately. [Banks, Credit Unions]

  • 🍂 October - November → Source: State Grants → Action: Search state websites and ask City/County offices about state pass-through opportunities.

  • ❄ Late Fall / Early Winter → Source: Local Grants → Action: Contact the Office of Community Development.

✔ FINAL CHECK

Before applying for your first grant:

  • Are you registered in SAM.gov and Grants.gov?

  • Have you claimed your GuideStar/Candid profile?

  • Have you identified your County’s CDBG portal?

  • Have you filed a FOIA request to see a winning application from last year?

  • Is your calendar marked for the upcoming Local, State, Federal, Corporate Grant, & Foundation funding windows?

title: Action Plan for Your Nonprofit: Partnerships & Funding
body:
✅ STRATEGIC PARTNERSHIPS & ADVANCED FUNDING

Course Checklist & Action Guide

This phase moves beyond basic registration into building the relationships, data, and assets required to secure sustainable funding.

🤝 Step 1: Establish Partnerships

Funding often follows collaboration. You need a strategy for who you work with.

  • Action: Define your partnership goals. Are you looking for program partners (to do the work with) or funding partners (to pay for the work)?

  • Action: Create a standard "Partnership Agreement" template.

⭕ Step 2: Map Your Stakeholders (The Circle Chart)

Identify everyone in your orbit using Megan’s Circle Chart method.

  • Clients: Who do you serve?

  • Peers: Who works in your space?

  • Businesses: Who has the funding?

  • Serve: Where can you volunteer to build goodwill?

  • Connect/Network: Who are the connectors?

🌟 Step 3: Update GuideStar (Candid)

If you created this in the previous phase, now is the time to optimize it for the "Platinum" seal.

  • Action: Ensure your profile includes recent financial data and demographic info.

🌟 Step 4: Monitor Charity Navigator

Donors use this to vet you.

  • Action: Check your "Encompass Rating" (for smaller nonprofits) or your Star Rating. Ensure your "Impact & Results" section is filled out.

🌟 Step 5: Register with Policy Commons

  • Action: If your nonprofit deals with research, policy, or advocacy, ensure you are listed here to be visible to academic and government funders.

📊 Step 6: Gather Data (Online Resources)

You must prove the "Need" exists. Use these specific resources to build your case:

  • Philanthropic Resources: Carnegie Corporation of New York

  • Social Determinants of Health: Healthy People 2030

  • State Health Disparities: Search your State’s Dept of Public Health (ex., California Office of Health Equity).

  • Economic Disparity: Use the Gini Index (World Bank) to show wealth inequality.

  • Reference: The State of Health Disparities (NCBI)

💰 Step 7: Budgeting & Financials

  • Action: Create a Master Operating Budget (overhead/admin).

  • Action: Create Program-Specific Budgets (restricted funds).

📜 Step 8: Governing Documents

  • Bylaws: Ensure they are up to date and signed.

  • MOUs: Draft Memorandums of Understanding for the partnerships identified in Step #1.

🎓 Step 9: Grant Lists & Lessons

Understand the landscape before applying.

  • Nonprofit vs. For-Profit Grants: Know the difference (Tax-exempt mission vs. Economic development).

  • Where to find Nonprofit Grants: GrantStation, Grants.gov, Foundation Directory Online.

  • Sponsorship vs. Grant:

    • Sponsorship: Marketing dollars. They want logo placement and audience eyeballs.

    • Grant: Philanthropic dollars. They want social impact and outcomes.

  • Funding Scope:

    • Sponsorships fund: Events, t-shirts, galas, media… your imagination is the limit.

    • Grants fund: Salaries, rent, direct program costs, supplies.

🎁 Step 10: In-Kind Giving Strategy

  • Action: Identify what you need that isn't cash (computers, office space, legal advice).

  • Action: Create a standard receipt for in-kind donations.

🗓 Step 11: The 2026 Grant Calendar

  • Action: Create a 12-month timeline.

  • Action: Plot the release dates for Local (Winter), State (Fall), Federal (Summer), and Corporate (Jan) opportunities. (There is no hard rule for this, but this is a good way to start creating your Grant Calendar.)

📄 Step 12: Create a Prospectus

Stop asking for "money" and start selling "opportunities."

  • What it is: An outline of the who, what, where, when, and why of what your nonprofit is doing, for each program you're running. A prospectus answers this one question, "Is doing this worth consideration?"

  • Why you need one: A grant prospectus serves as a professional 'first date' document that allows a funder to quickly determine if your mission aligns with their goals before anyone invests time in a full proposal.

    • How It Differs From Related Documents

      • Proposal: Asks for something specific.

      • Business plan: Operational and internal.

      • One-pager: High-level snapshot.

      • Prospectus: Strategic, comprehensive, and decision-ready.

  • Action: Identify the Who, What, Where, When, and Why of ALL your Nonprofit's programs.

📣 Step 13: Media Outreach Strategies

  • Action: Build a press list of local journalists who cover your topic.

  • Action: Draft a template press release for when you win your first grant.

✔ FINAL CHECK

  • Do you have your stakeholder circle filled out?

  • Are your data sources bookmarked for your next proposal?

  • Do you understand the difference between what a sponsor funds vs. a grant?

  • Is your 2026 Calendar ready?

title: Contact These 10 Key Organizations
body:
It’s time for the next steps after your free business mentor appointment, and you understand your business goals and potential funding sources.

This lesson focuses on contacting organizations that offer grants and financial assistance to help you start or grow your business. These programs provide funding, training, and resources for entrepreneurs.

 1. Watch Matthews's video first! 

These programs are part of the "giving economy"—a network of government offices and nonprofits distributing funds for free. Unlike for-profit websites you might find on Google, these organizations exist to help you, not to charge you for services.

 2. Contact These 10 Key Organizations 

  1.  ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT OFFICES  Visit eda.gov/resources to find your state’s economic development office. These offices distribute grants, loans, and training programs to help businesses grow. Call for funding opportunities in your state.

  2.  APEX ACCELERATORS  Visit apexaccelerators.us to connect with APEX Accelerators, a government-funded program that helps businesses secure government contracts—a long-term funding source for your business.

  3.  SSBCI (State Small Business Credit Initiative) Visit home.treasury.gov to locate your state’s SSBCI program, which provides grants, loans, and direct investments in small businesses. 

  4.  CAREERONESTOP  (DEPARTMENT OF LABOR) Visit careeronestop.org to access training grants and funding for entrepreneurs. This program can help train employees or provide funding for you to learn new skills. Please Visit the CareerOneStop Business Center.

  5.  CDFIs  (Community Development Financial Institutions) Use the CDFI locator at cdfifund.gov to find government-backed banks that provide grants and low-interest loans to small businesses.

  6.  OPPORTUNITY NETWORK  (MATCHED SAVINGS GRANTS) Some organizations match your savings—if you save $1, they add $5 or more to fund your business. Visit cdfifund.gov to find programs in your area.

  7.  VETERAN-OWNED BUSINESS ASSISTANCE  If you’re a veteran, there are special grants and funding programs to support your business. Visit sba.gov to find Veteran Business Outreach Centers near you.

  8.  MINORITY & WOMEN-OWNED BUSINESS SUPPORT  There are dedicated grants for women and minority entrepreneurs available through state and nonprofit programs. Visit grants.gov to check eligibility.

  9.  MEETUP.COM FOR ENTREPRENEURS  Networking is essential. Use meetup.com to find local entrepreneur groups and connect with mentors, investors, and fellow business owners. 

  10.  LOCAL SMALL BUSINESS DEVELOPMENT CENTERS  (SBDCs) Visit americassbdc.org to find Small Business Development Centers (SBDCs) that provide free business coaching, funding advice, and resources for entrepreneurs.

 TIP: How to Approach These Organizations 

  • 📞 CALL FIRST: Most grants require direct contact before applying. Call and explain your business idea.

  • 💪 BE PERSISTENT: Some programs might not be available in your area. Keep asking until you find the right fit.

  • 🎯 AVOID GOOGLE SCAMS: Many for-profit companies charge fees for grant applications—stick to nonprofit and government-backed resources.

START CALLING NOW☟

  • 🔗 State Economic Development Agencies

  • 🔗 APEX Accelerators

  • 🔗 SSBCI Program

  • 🔗 CareerOneStop

  • 🔗 CDFI Locator

  • 🔗 Opportunity Programs

  • 🔗 Veterans Business Outreach Center (VBOC)

  • 🔗 Grants for Women & Minorities

  • 🔗 Meetup.com

  • 🔗 Small Business Development Centers (SBDCs)

This step sets you on the path to securing the funds you need for your business. Start calling today! 🚀

Overview of Walmart’s giving initiatives for nonprofits and businesses making local impact.

body:
Being a woman in business comes with unique challenges—but also incredible opportunities. Across the U.S. and beyond, there are grants, fellowships, loans, and programs designed specifically to support women-owned businesses at every stage. Whether you're launching a startup, growing your boutique, or leading in tech—there’s help waiting for you.

Here’s your curated guide to funding, certifications, and resources built to help female founders thrive.

title: Grants & Support for Minority Groups
body:
If you're a business owner from a minority background or part of an underserved community, there are powerful resources available to support your growth. These include free business centers, mentorship, targeted grants, retail partnerships, and national accelerators—many of which are not widely known.

This lesson pulls together the best options for support, funding, and certification to help you thrive.

🏢 Business Centers & Support Services

These organizations provide direct, hands-on help—from business planning and funding prep to certification support and federal contract guidance.

🔹 MBDA Business Centers

Connect with a local Minority Business Development Agency (MBDA) center for strategic support, grant navigation, and growth opportunities.

🔹 MBDA Business Resources

Full directory of tools, partners, and federal programs for minority-owned businesses.

🔹 SBA: Minority-Owned Business Guide

Explore how the Small Business Administration supports minority business owners through funding, certifications, and development programs.

🔹 Center for Micro-Entrepreneurial Training

A practical, hands-on support center for micro-businesses and early-stage entrepreneurs from underserved communities.

💸 Grants & Funding for Minority Entrepreneurs

These opportunities are tailored specifically to Black, Latino, Indigenous, and other underrepresented business owners. Some offer funding, while others provide training and visibility.

🔹 Capital Readiness Program – MBDA

Supports entrepreneurs in preparing for investment and funding with business development training and capital access.

🔹 NAACP Powershift Entrepreneur Grant

Direct grant support for Black entrepreneurs with scalable business ideas.

🔹 Amazon Black Business Accelerator

Exclusive access to funding, training, and marketing support for Black-owned brands selling on Amazon.

🔹 Rebuild The Block

Emergency grants and community funding for Black entrepreneurs.

🔹 Galaxy Grants

Small business funding with a focus on women and minority founders.

🔹 Operation Hope – 1 Million Black Businesses

A national initiative to launch and grow Black-owned businesses, offering coaching, training, and support.

🔹 Gold House Ventures

Resources and funding for Asian and Pacific Islander founders through venture capital and mentorship.

🔹 Retail Readiness Program – Watson

Helps underrepresented entrepreneurs get ready to pitch, scale, and distribute through retail partnerships.

🔹 Pathway to Opportunity

Grant and mentorship platform focused on Black, Latino, and underserved entrepreneurs.

🔹 Black Ambition

Major funding and mentorship prize for innovative Black and Latinx-led businesses.

🔹 The Grant – TRANSFORM

Funds projects that center justice, racial equity, and systemic change in underserved communities.

🔹 Scale-Up Pitch Challenge – NBMBAA

Pitch competition for Black MBA entrepreneurs, offering exposure and investment.

🔹 2024 Support Latino Business Impact Fund

Funding opportunity for Latino-owned businesses with community-focused missions.

🔹 Juntos Crecemos – PepsiCo

Marketing and business development support for Latino small businesses in the food and beverage industry.

🔹 Wish Local Empowerment Program

Microgrants and visibility for underrepresented small businesses that sell locally.

title: Your First Steps to Start a Business Legally
body:
Before you dive into applying for grants, building a brand, or launching your product—there are a few foundational steps you must take to officially set up your business.

This checklist will guide you through the essential legal and administrative actions needed to start strong. It includes everything from choosing your business structure to opening a bank account and securing licenses.

💡 Important: In the United States, all business registrations and incorporations are handled on the state level. This means that fees, processes, and specific requirements vary depending on your state.
We highly recommend checking with your state’s Department of Commerce or Secretary of State to confirm details specific to your location.

✅ Business Start-Up Checklist

Each item builds on the one before. Read through each step carefully and keep track of your progress. Items marked with * need to be renewed annually. Items marked with *? may have unique renewal timelines—check locally.

☐ 1. Select Your Business Name & Legal Structure

Decide on your business name and legal form: Sole Proprietorship, Partnership, LLC, or Corporation. This choice affects taxes, liability, and how you can raise funds.

☐ 2. Research Your Business Name with the Secretary of State

Research Business Name with your state’s Secretary of State’s website to make sure no other business has that name.

☐ 3. Register the Legal Entity with Your State *

File your business with the state government and obtain your Certificate of Incorporation or Articles of Organization.

☐ 4. Get Your State Tax License and Set Up Tax Accounts

Create a State Tax ID/account through your state’s tax division. This is different from your federal EIN and is essential for state-level tax compliance.

☐ 5. Obtain Your Federal EIN from the IRS

Apply online for your Employer Identification Number (EIN) from the IRS. This is necessary to open bank accounts, hire employees, and file taxes.
👉 Apply for an EIN here

☐ 6. Open a Business Bank or Credit Union Account

Set up a business checking account at a trusted FDIC-insured bank or credit union using your EIN and state paperwork.

☐ 7. Apply for a Local Business License *

Depending on your location, you’ll need to register your business with your city or county office based on your physical address.

☐ 8. Get Professional Licenses or Permits (if required) *?

If your business operates in a regulated industry (like health, finance, childcare, or food services), you may need specific licenses or inspections.
📌 Renewal timelines vary. Always verify the terms for your specific license or permit.


Download your checklist here

💬 Need help verifying your next step?

📣 Your Next Move

title: Governement Contracting for Small Businesses
body:
Did you know that the U.S. government is the largest buyer of goods and services in the world? Every year, billions of dollars in contracts are awarded to small businesses—just like yours. Whether you offer products, services, consulting, or manufacturing, government contracting can open a stable and lucrative revenue stream.

But breaking into federal, state, or local contracting requires understanding the process, registering correctly, and knowing where to look. This guide will walk you through the essential steps and tools to get started.

1⃣ Register Your Business on SAM.gov (Your First Step)

Before you can bid on federal contracts or subcontracts, you must register your business on SAM.gov. This is the official database where all contractors are listed.

  • 🔹 Entity Checklist
    Before registering, download the Entity Checklist (PDF) on SAM.gov to prepare all required documents.

  • 🔹 Search Contracts
    Even before you're fully registered, browse available contracts to get familiar with opportunities.

👉 Start here: SAM.gov Registration & Search

2⃣ Know Your Codes: NAICS, PSC & UNSPSC

Government agencies use specific codes to classify businesses and their services/products. You’ll need these during registration and bidding.

  • 🔹 NAICS Codes
    The North American Industry Classification System assigns a 6-digit number to describe your industry.

    • 🔹The following resources have both free and for-cost services. Please stick to the free resources:

      • 🔹https://www.naics.com/

      • 🔹https://naicscode.com/ 

  • 🔹 PSC Codes
    Product Service Codes (PSC) describe exactly what goods or services you're offering.

  • 🔹 UNSPSC Codes
    Some agencies may also require UNSPSC Codes for additional classification.

💡 Make sure you’ve identified the correct codes before completing your SAM registration.

3⃣ Get Support from APEX Accelerators

You don’t have to navigate government contracting alone. APEX Accelerators (formerly PTACs) offer free counseling to help small businesses understand and succeed in federal contracting.

  • 🔹 Learn how to bid

  • 🔹 Understand compliance rules

  • 🔹 Get help with certifications

👉 Find a counselor near you: APEX Accelerators

4⃣ Use SBA Tools & Programs

The U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA) offers powerful tools to help you access set-aside contracts and navigate the system.

  • 🔹 Size Standards Tool
    Check if your business qualifies as a “small business” for federal contracting purposes.
    Use the Tool

  • 🔹 SBA Contracting Assistance Programs
    Explore programs like 8(a), HUBZone, and WOSB certifications to access exclusive contract opportunities.
    Learn More

5⃣ Payment Systems: PIEE & More

If you're contracting with the Department of Defense or its agencies, you’ll likely need to register on the Procurement Integrated Enterprise Environment (PIEE) to receive payments.

For other agencies, payment systems will vary—always confirm with the awarding agency which platform to use.

6⃣ Learn the Rules: Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR)

The Federal Acquisition Regulation (FAR) outlines how federal contracts are issued and managed. It’s complex, so reviewing it with an APEX Accelerator counselor is highly recommended.

7⃣ Research & Forecasting Tools

Get ahead by knowing what agencies are buying and who they’re buying from:

  • 🔹 Agency Recurring Procurement Forecasts
    See what agencies plan to purchase in upcoming cycles.

  • 🔹 USA Spending
    Track past contracts—who won them and for how much.

  • 🔹 D-U-N-S Number
    While no longer required for SAM.gov, many other agencies still ask for a D-U-N-S number. It’s like a Social Security number for your business—good to have on hand.

📣 Your Next Move


1⃣ Gather your documents using the SAM.gov Entity Checklist.

2⃣ Identify your NAICS, PSC, and (if needed) UNSPSC codes.

3⃣ Register on SAM.gov and book a free session with your local APEX Accelerator counselor.

4⃣ Explore SBA’s contracting assistance programs to see if you qualify for set-asides.

💡 Government contracting can feel overwhelming at first—but with the right steps and support, it becomes a powerful way to grow your business.

✔ Once you're registered and familiar with the process, start bidding on smaller contracts to build experience—and watch new doors open!

title: Accelerators, Incubators & Angel Investors
body:
If you’re looking for growth support, mentorship, funding—or all three—these platforms and programs can help you take your business idea to the next level. Whether you're an early-stage startup or ready to scale, these are some of the best places to start.

💡 Startup Accelerators & Incubators

  • AngelPad
    A boutique accelerator for seed-stage startups in tech, product, and SaaS.

  • Techstars
    Global startup accelerator with industry-specific programs and a powerful mentor network.

  • Startup School by Y Combinator
    Free online program with tools and weekly mentorship for founders at any stage.

  • Tech Ranch Austin
    Entrepreneur community and incubator based in Austin, focused on impact-driven startups.

  • MassChallenge
    A no-equity accelerator that supports high-impact, early-stage startups across sectors.

  • New Venture Challenge – Polsky Center
    University of Chicago’s top-tier accelerator with $1M+ in investments each year.

  • Main Street Ventures
    Provides capital, connections, and resources to early-stage entrepreneurs in underserved areas.

  • Mucker Capital Accelerator
    Invests and works hands-on with companies at the earliest stages outside of Silicon Valley.

    A 12-week accelerator for early and growth-stage fintech startups with enterprise potential.

    Connects entrepreneurs with a global network of private investors.

    A platform that links small businesses with angel investors across the U.S.

    Online network for entrepreneurs, investors, advisors, and business partners.

💼 Non-Traditional Business Funding

Not every great idea fits the mold—and not every business needs a bank loan or venture capital to grow. Non-traditional funding opens doors through alternative pathways like crowdfunding, pitch competitions, revenue-based financing, community development funds, peer-to-peer lending, and even business grants from brands or nonprofits.

These options often provide more flexibility, less pressure, and a stronger alignment with mission-driven or underserved entrepreneurs—making them ideal for founders who want creative capital without giving up control.

How to Get Ready

BE ON TIME | Join a few minutes early so you don't miss the tour

CAMERA ON | Keep your camera on if you feel comfortable

COME CURIOUS | Bring any questions you have about the community

TAKE NOTES | Write down helpful tips so you can easily find them later
